json.draft: We searched alpha, beta and gamma (exports imported 2026-10-20) with a Boolean query (synonym blocks version 1, frozen), developed against 4 known-relevant development papers and tested once on 2 held-out validation papers. Seed papers were split into a development set and a validation set. Where the validation papers came from: 2 added by the researcher. Recall on the validation set: 2 of 2, 95% interval 0.16 to 1.00. 2 validation papers were also found by the query. The searches returned 74 records; deduplication by DOI, exact title and corroborated fuzzy title matching, with 11 uncertain pairs decided by hand left 39 unique records. Records were ranked by their similarity to one anchor sentence per construct cell (anchors version 1, mean of the top 2 cells) using the embedding model BAAI/bge-m3. A band-stratified probability sample of 16 records across the ranking and a purposive development set of 16 records were labelled by 1 reviewer. Each development sample record needed one reviewer's final label. Titles and abstracts were screened by gpt-4o-mini against a codebook of 4 elements; every grade had to be supported by a verbatim quote, and a record was excluded only when the construct was shown to be absent or the study unrelated. Two independent reads with a blind third read on disagreement were combined by a 2-of-3 majority (protocol main): 18 records were included and 4 kept for full-text reading, of 39 screened. Every pass (pass A, pass B and the judge) used gpt-4o-mini. Passes A, B and the judge use the same model (gpt-4o-mini, temperature 0): their readings are not independent. Against the human labels of the probability sample, the band-weighted recall of the screening (lenient variant) was 1.00 (95% interval 0.54 to 1.00, Kish effective size method; 7 relevant validation papers). Recall on validation was seen for 2 result sets with different settings (sets 1, 2); choosing between them on this sample uses it for model selection. No recall target was set in advance. The first draw is systematic and is treated as random within each band; the guarantee at every look assumes a random draw (an open question). The bounds are conservative: the error is split over every band and screening decision and each is bounded on its own, so they may need substantially more labels than a sharper method to show the same result. This estimate covers 27 ranked records (not the 6 records with too short an abstract, or the 6 seed papers), screened on title and abstract only; it says nothing about full-text screening. No independent second review was done; one reviewer labelled the samples. The procedure, prompts, run specifications and all numbers are reproducible from the project with WIDER (protocol hash 19f81d9dcb7a).

json.draft: We searched alpha, beta and gamma (exports imported 2026-10-20) with a Boolean query (synonym blocks version 1, frozen), developed against 4 known-relevant development papers and tested once on 2 held-out validation papers. Seed papers were split into a development set and a validation set. Where the validation papers came from: 2 added by the researcher. Recall on the validation set: 2 of 2, 95% interval 0.16 to 1.00. 2 validation papers were also found by the query. The searches returned 74 records; deduplication by DOI, exact title and corroborated fuzzy title matching, with 11 uncertain pairs decided by hand left 39 unique records. Records were ranked by their similarity to one anchor sentence per construct cell (anchors version 1, mean of the top 2 cells) using the embedding model BAAI/bge-m3. A band-stratified probability sample of 16 records across the ranking and a purposive development set of 16 records were labelled by 1 reviewer. Each development sample record needed one reviewer's final label. No independent second review was done; one reviewer labelled the samples. The procedure, prompts, run specifications and all numbers are reproducible from the project with WIDER (protocol hash 19f81d9dcb7a).

sections.text: What leads employees to speak up, stay silent or report problems upward or outward at work, and what follows when they do?
sections.title: Question

sections.text: Empirical studies of employees who voluntarily raise suggestions, concerns or problems with someone who could act on them (a supervisor, senior management, an internal or external authority), or who withhold such input, where the study measures what predicts that behaviour or what follows from it.
sections.title: Target description

items: Voice, silence or reporting behaviour: The study measures employees speaking up, withholding input, or reporting problems.
Discretionary and directed upward or outward: The behaviour is the employee's own choice and is directed at someone who could act on it.
Antecedents or consequences are studied: The study relates the behaviour to predictors, reactions or outcomes.
Employees in work organisations: The actors are employees, members or contractors of an organisation.
sections.title: Elements

items: voice_antecedent: what leads employees to speak up with suggestions or concerns
voice_consequence: how receivers react to voice and what follows for the speaker
silence_antecedent: why employees withhold concerns or opinions
silence_consequence: what follows when employees stay silent
whistleblowing_antecedent: what leads employees to report irregularities to an authority
whistleblowing_consequence: what happens to employees after they report irregularities
sections.title: Cells

items: Is voice only one sub-dimension of a broader scale that is not analysed separately? (if yes: maybe)
Does the study examine only a formal participation scheme or procedure? (if yes: maybe)
sections.title: Checks

items: reviews and conceptual papers on the topic (default: maybe)
qualitative studies with no measured antecedent or outcome (default: maybe)
sections.title: Edge cases

items: a: no voice, silence or reporting behaviour measured
b: not discretionary or not directed at someone who could act
c: no antecedent or consequence studied
d: actors are not employees
e: not empirical
f: too little information
sections.title: Exclusion reasons

items: setting or industry
occupation
country
research method
sections.title: Not a criterion

items: participation schemes and industrial democracy (works councils, codetermination)
grievance procedures as a formal channel
organisational citizenship behaviour composites
psychological safety as a climate construct
customer and consumer complaining
citizen participation and political voice
peer information sharing and team communication
sections.title: Adjacent literatures

sections.text: A record with no usable abstract is maybe unless the title alone settles it.
sections.title: Thin abstracts

items: Press Ask WIDER in the top bar, or pick the "Ask WIDER" tab beside "Guide" in the side panel. "Asking about:" names the page you are on (change it, or pick "WIDER in general"); with no name set yet, type it in "Your name" there (afterwards Change beside "Working as" in the top bar changes it); type a question and press Ask. The answer is drawn from WIDER's own documents (the guide, the methods and the glossary), with its sources under it; it can be wrong, so check them. From the command line: `wider assistant ask "<question>" [--page <page>]`.

It reads the page's guide, WIDER's documents, your project's settings and stage status, and your earlier questions. It never reads a record, a label, a note or a model's decision, and it is not offered while a labelling queue shows records.

Your conversation is kept on this computer, in the project's `assistant/` folder, one file per name, and never goes into a share bundle or replication package. Forget this conversation deletes yours (`wider assistant forget`).
If an answer did not help, press Didn't help under it (`wider assistant unhelpful <turn>`); `wider assistant history --unanswered` lists those questions so WIDER's documents can be improved.

queue.title_b: Speaking up in the cockpit: first officers and error reporting

stages.description: Write down the research question(s), the inclusion and exclusion notes, the seed papers (a development and a validation set), and the databases you will search. Everything later is checked against these inputs.
stages.title: Review plan
stages.why: A review of a broad construct drifts unless the question and the known-relevant papers are fixed first; the validation seed papers are held back so the search can be tested once, honestly.

stages.description: The LLM proposes, from your question and the development seed papers' abstracts, the construct cells, the screening codebook, synonym blocks for the query, one anchor sentence per cell, and near-miss (adjacent literature) descriptions. You edit and approve each; every version is kept.
stages.title: Concepts and synonyms
stages.why: Broad constructs are reviewed well only when their vocabulary and boundaries are written down before searching; grounding the proposals in your own seed papers keeps them specific to your literature.

stages.description: The approved synonym blocks are rendered into one Boolean string per chosen database, in that database's own syntax. You run the searches yourself and bring back the exports. Coverage of the development seed papers is checked while you edit; the validation set is reported only once the query is frozen or the uploads are marked final.
stages.title: Search strings
stages.why: Databases differ in syntax and limits; one shared query representation keeps the strings consistent and reproducible, and the freeze rule prevents tuning the query to the test papers.

stages.description: Database exports (RIS, CSV/TSV, XLS/XLSX or BibTeX, one folder per database) are recognised by their header, standardised and stored with their source file; a file is imported once, by content hash, and gets a sanity verdict (ok, capped, off-topic, empty, duplicate). Coverage then shows which seed papers each database returned (by DOI, exact title, then fuzzy title) and, after dedup, which the corpus holds.
stages.title: Search results
stages.why: An export that is not the result of your query (wrong search, truncated download) silently ruins recall; a seed paper missing from the database that should have found it is the cheapest warning you will get.

stages.description: Records are merged by DOI, then exact title, then fuzzy title with corroboration (year, first author, journal). Uncertain pairs go to a manual queue; your decisions are stored and re-applied. PRISMA counts and audit files are written.
stages.title: Deduplication
stages.why: Rules alone over-merge or under-merge; a transparent queue with named rules makes the counts auditable.

stages.description: Records with a thin or missing abstract are completed from OpenAlex, Crossref, Europe PMC and Semantic Scholar in that order; nothing already present is overwritten and every fetch is logged.
stages.title: Missing abstracts
stages.why: Ranking and screening read the abstract; a record without one is judged on its title alone, so it is easily ranked low or set aside.

stages.description: Every record is embedded and scored against the approved anchors (mean of its top cells). The ranking sorts, never filters. Seed-paper ranks, recall@K and tests without one part over anchor versions and embedding models show how well the anchors work; clusters in the top of the ranking describe the topics found.
stages.title: Ranking
stages.why: A ranking lets the human and LLM effort concentrate where relevant papers are dense, while a probability sample over the whole ranking keeps the recall estimate honest.

stages.description: A band-stratified probability sample (for the recall estimate) and a purposive development set (likely includes, near-misses per adjacent literature, cluster medoids, thin abstracts, tail) are drawn and labelled in the blinded queue by one or two reviewers.
stages.title: Samples and labelling
stages.why: Human labels on a known design are what make the LLM's recall measurable; the development set is where the prompt is tuned on the hardest cases.

stages.description: The codebook becomes a prompt and JSON schema; each record is screened in an isolated call that quotes the words behind every grade, and an "absent" grade whose quote is not in the record becomes unclear. Development-set evaluation reports misses per adjacent literature; the corpus protocol runs two passes, a blind third read on disagreement and a second screen of the maybes.
stages.title: Screening
stages.why: Verbatim quotes and a recall-first rule keep a small model from excluding on a hunch; repeated reads and a blind third read on disagreement catch some of its slips, and show where it answers inconsistently.

stages.description: Band-weighted recall of the LLM screen against the human labels, with an interval and the number of relevant papers, the PRISMA flow and a shareable report without abstracts.
stages.title: Recall and report
stages.why: The claim a review makes is "we found nearly all of it"; this stage puts a number and an interval on it.

stages.description: Stage-2 extension point.
stages.title: Full-text screening
stages.why: Abstract-level screening leaves the includes and maybes; reading their full texts is the next decision layer.

stages.description: Stage-2 extension point.
stages.title: Data extraction
stages.why: Once the set is final, the same codebook elements can be extracted per paper for the synthesis.

stages.description: Stage-2 extension point.
stages.title: Synthesis
stages.why: The extracted elements are what a synthesis of a wide literature is built from.

method.text: The estimate weights each band's relevant labelled records by the band's records per labelled record and adds the bands up. The range bounds the kept and the not-kept records of each band apart, at a level that holds for all of them together at every look, and adds those bounds up, so it is wider and need not be centred on the estimate.

json.draft: We searched alpha, beta and gamma (exports imported 2026-10-20) with a Boolean query (synonym blocks version 1, frozen), developed against 4 known-relevant development papers and tested once on 2 held-out validation papers. Seed papers were split into a development set and a validation set. Where the validation papers came from: 2 added by the researcher. Recall on the validation set: 2 of 2, 95% interval 0.16 to 1.00. 2 validation papers were also found by the query. The searches returned 74 records; deduplication by DOI, exact title and corroborated fuzzy title matching, with 11 uncertain pairs decided by hand left 39 unique records. Records were ranked by their similarity to one anchor sentence per construct cell (anchors version 1, mean of the top 2 cells) using the embedding model BAAI/bge-m3. A band-stratified probability sample of 16 records across the ranking and a purposive development set of 16 records were labelled by 1 reviewer. Each development sample record needed one reviewer's final label. Titles and abstracts were screened by gpt-4o-mini against a codebook of 4 elements; every grade had to be supported by a verbatim quote, and a record was excluded only when the construct was shown to be absent or the study unrelated. Two independent reads with a blind third read on disagreement were combined by a 2-of-3 majority (protocol main): 18 records were included and 4 kept for full-text reading, of 39 screened. Every pass (pass A, pass B and the judge) used gpt-4o-mini. Passes A, B and the judge use the same model (gpt-4o-mini, temperature 0): their readings are not independent. Against the human labels of the probability sample, the band-weighted recall of the screening (lenient variant) was 1.00 (95% interval 0.54 to 1.00, Kish effective size method; 7 relevant validation papers). No recall target was set in advance. The first draw is systematic and is treated as random within each band; the guarantee at every look assumes a random draw (an open question). The bounds are conservative: the error is split over every band and screening decision and each is bounded on its own, so they may need substantially more labels than a sharper method to show the same result. This estimate covers 27 ranked records (not the 6 records with too short an abstract, or the 6 seed papers), screened on title and abstract only; it says nothing about full-text screening. No independent second review was done; one reviewer labelled the samples. The procedure, prompts, run specifications and all numbers are reproducible from the project with WIDER (protocol hash 19f81d9dcb7a).

catalogue.label: PubMed

catalogue.description: Web-scale academic search with a short query limit; useful as a check, not as a corpus source.
catalogue.label: Google Scholar (reduced string)
catalogue.paste: Google Scholar accepts about 256 characters, no truncation and no proximity. The reduced string keeps as many terms of each required block as fit, trimming the longest block first, a truncated term without its `*`; when even one term per block is too long, the last blocks are left out. Excluded (NOT) blocks are left out too. Use it for a quick check, not for the corpus.

stages.description: Write down the research question(s), the inclusion and exclusion notes, the seed papers (a development and a validation set), and the databases you will search. Everything later is checked against these inputs.
stages.title: Review plan
stages.why: A review of a broad construct drifts unless the question and the known-relevant papers are fixed first; the validation seed papers are held back so the search can be tested once, honestly.

stages.description: The LLM proposes, from your question and the development seed papers' abstracts, the construct cells, the screening codebook, synonym blocks for the query, one anchor sentence per cell, and near-miss (adjacent literature) descriptions. You edit and approve each; every version is kept.
stages.title: Concepts and synonyms
stages.why: Broad constructs are reviewed well only when their vocabulary and boundaries are written down before searching; grounding the proposals in your own seed papers keeps them specific to your literature.

stages.description: The approved synonym blocks are rendered into one Boolean string per chosen database, in that database's own syntax. You run the searches yourself and bring back the exports. Coverage of the development seed papers is checked while you edit; the validation set is reported only once the query is frozen or the uploads are marked final.
stages.title: Search strings
stages.why: Databases differ in syntax and limits; one shared query representation keeps the strings consistent and reproducible, and the freeze rule prevents tuning the query to the test papers.

stages.description: Database exports (RIS, CSV/TSV, XLS/XLSX or BibTeX, one folder per database) are recognised by their header, standardised and stored with their source file; a file is imported once, by content hash, and gets a sanity verdict (ok, capped, off-topic, empty, duplicate). Coverage then shows which seed papers each database returned (by DOI, exact title, then fuzzy title) and, after dedup, which the corpus holds.
stages.title: Search results
stages.why: An export that is not the result of your query (wrong search, truncated download) silently ruins recall; a seed paper missing from the database that should have found it is the cheapest warning you will get.

stages.description: Records are merged by DOI, then exact title, then fuzzy title with corroboration (year, first author, journal). Uncertain pairs go to a manual queue; your decisions are stored and re-applied. PRISMA counts and audit files are written.
stages.title: Deduplication
stages.why: Rules alone over-merge or under-merge; a transparent queue with named rules makes the counts auditable.

stages.description: Records with a thin or missing abstract are completed from OpenAlex, Crossref, Europe PMC and Semantic Scholar in that order; nothing already present is overwritten and every fetch is logged.
stages.title: Missing abstracts
stages.why: Ranking and screening read the abstract; a record without one is judged on its title alone, so it is easily ranked low or set aside.

stages.description: Every record is embedded and scored against the approved anchors (mean of its top cells). The ranking sorts, never filters. Seed-paper ranks, recall@K and tests without one part over anchor versions and embedding models show how well the anchors work; clusters in the top of the ranking describe the topics found.
stages.title: Ranking
stages.why: A ranking lets the human and LLM effort concentrate where relevant papers are dense, while a probability sample over the whole ranking keeps the recall estimate honest.

stages.description: A band-stratified probability sample (for the recall estimate) and a purposive development set (likely includes, near-misses per adjacent literature, cluster medoids, thin abstracts, tail) are drawn and labelled in the blinded queue by one or two reviewers.
stages.title: Samples and labelling
stages.why: Human labels on a known design are what make the LLM's recall measurable; the development set is where the prompt is tuned on the hardest cases.

stages.description: The codebook becomes a prompt and JSON schema; each record is screened in an isolated call that quotes the words behind every grade, and an "absent" grade whose quote is not in the record becomes unclear. Development-set evaluation reports misses per adjacent literature; the corpus protocol runs two passes, a blind third read on disagreement and a second screen of the maybes.
stages.title: Screening
stages.why: Verbatim quotes and a recall-first rule keep a small model from excluding on a hunch; repeated reads and a blind third read on disagreement catch some of its slips, and show where it answers inconsistently.

stages.description: Band-weighted recall of the LLM screen against the human labels, with an interval and the number of relevant papers, the PRISMA flow and a shareable report without abstracts.
stages.title: Recall and report
stages.why: The claim a review makes is "we found nearly all of it"; this stage puts a number and an interval on it.

stages.description: Stage-2 extension point.
stages.title: Full-text screening
stages.why: Abstract-level screening leaves the includes and maybes; reading their full texts is the next decision layer.

stages.description: Stage-2 extension point.
stages.title: Data extraction
stages.why: Once the set is final, the same codebook elements can be extracted per paper for the synthesis.

stages.description: Stage-2 extension point.
stages.title: Synthesis
stages.why: The extracted elements are what a synthesis of a wide literature is built from.

json.prompt:
You are helping a researcher write the **screening codebook** for a systematic literature review: the frozen rules that human and machine screeners will apply to every title and abstract. The codebook decides what counts, so it must be explicit about elements, adjacent literatures that look like matches but are not, and edge cases.

# The review

Research question:
- What leads employees to speak up, stay silent or report problems at work, and what follows when they do?

# Development benchmark papers

These 4 papers are known to belong in the review. They are the evidence for every proposal you make:
ground your proposals in what these papers study, how they describe it, and the words they use.

## [B1] Speaking up to supervisors: what makes service employees offer suggestions

(no abstract available)


## [B2] Why nurses keep patient-safety concerns to themselves

(no abstract available)


## [B3] Middle managers selling issues to top management

(no abstract available)


## [B4] Speaking up in the cockpit: first officers and error reporting

(no abstract available)

# Cells already defined by the researcher

  concerns and problems by employees.'

- name: focus

  - key: consequence

- setting or industry

# What to produce

- `question`: the screening question in one sentence.
- `target_description`: one paragraph describing the kind of study we are looking for: typical designs, who the actors are and who else is involved, the settings, the outcomes, and the ways the key variable can enter (main variable, one predictor among several, covariate).
- `elements`: two to six elements that must all be plausibly present for a record to be eligible. Each has an id (e1, e2, ...), a name, a rule sentence, `counts` (what satisfies it) and `does_not_count` (what does not). Derive them from what every benchmark paper has in common.
- `exclusion_reasons`: one short-coded reason per element (a, b, c, ...), each naming the element it maps to, plus "not empirical" and "too little information".
- `adjacent_literatures`: literatures that are retrieved by the same search terms and look like includes but are not, each with the element it strains, the decision (exclude / include / maybe) and the reason code. Also list boundary cases that are included with a code. Aim for eight to twelve.
- `checks`: three to six yes/no questions a screener must answer before deciding, each with what follows if the answer is yes. These settle the recurring hard cases.
- `edge_cases`: two to five cases the researcher must decide before the first label, each with a recommended default.
- `labels`: label groups applied to includes (for example cell, the role of the parties involved, how the key variable entered), each with its values. Use the cell keys above if cells are defined.
- `thin_abstract_rule`: what to do when there is no abstract or fewer than about 20 words.

The rule of the codebook is recall first: a wrong exclusion is lost for good, a wrong inclusion costs one full-text read. Write every rule so that doubt resolves to "maybe", never to "exclude".

json.abstract: We measured organisational citizenship behaviour in 120 retail stores with a combined scale that covers helping colleagues, following rules and making suggestions. Stores with higher citizenship scores had higher sales the following year.
json.authors: Dalby, B.; Esposito, C.; Farrow, D.
json.title: Citizenship behaviour and team performance in retail stores

json.abstract: We surveyed 300 care workers about whether they raised concerns about care quality with their supervisor. Newcomers raised concerns less often than staff with longer tenure, and having an assigned mentor reduced the gap.
json.title: Newcomers and raising concerns in social care

json.abstract: This case description explains how a mid-sized insurer set up a programme to encourage staff to speak up, including training for managers and a monthly feedback forum. We describe the steps taken and the lessons the company drew.
json.title: Building a speak-up programme: a company's experience

json.abstract: A survey of 650 employees compared how often people working from home and in the office raised concerns with their manager. Employees working from home raised fewer concerns, but the gap closed when they had a weekly one-to-one video call.
json.authors: Bello, D.; Corvin, E.; Dalby, F.
json.title: Working from home and raising concerns with the manager

json.abstract: A multilevel study of 70 software teams found that team members offered more suggestions to leaders who admitted their own mistakes. Feeling safe to take interpersonal risks explained part of this link.
json.title: Humble leaders and employee suggestions in software firms

json.abstract: Using data from 18 small economies, we show how changes in central bank interest rates pass through to inflation.
json.authors: Corvin, G.; Dalby, H.; Esposito, A.
json.title: Interest rates and inflation in small open economies

json.abstract: We studied how union representatives in 30 workplaces put members' complaints on the agenda of formal consultation meetings with management. Complaints raised in writing before the meeting were resolved more often.
json.title: Union representatives raising members' complaints in formal meetings

json.abstract: We developed a six-item scale of how often employees make suggestions at work and tested it in two samples of 300 and 450 employees. The items formed one factor, and scores correlated moderately with job satisfaction, which we report as evidence of validity.
json.title: A short scale for measuring employee suggestions

json.abstract: Field trials over ten years found more carbon in the top soil layer of fields farmed without ploughing.
json.title: Soil carbon under no-till farming

json.abstract: Interviews with 45 nursing and engineering students on work placements asked whether they told a supervisor when they saw unsafe practice. Students spoke up when their placement supervisor had asked for feedback early on and stayed silent when they feared a poor placement grade.
json.authors: Kowal, G.; Lindqvist, H.; Moreau, A.
json.title: Students on work placements speaking up about unsafe practice

json.abstract: We report a catalyst that produces ammonia at lower pressure than current methods and test it over 500 hours.
json.authors: Jansen, D.; Kowal, E.; Lindqvist, F.
json.title: A new catalyst for ammonia production

json.abstract: Observers recorded how often team members in 48 surgical teams pointed out possible errors during operations. Team members spoke up more often in teams whose surgeon had introduced everyone by name at the start, and errors were caught earlier in those teams.
json.title: Speaking up about errors in surgical teams

json.abstract: An online survey of 1,100 shoppers found that a quick and friendly response to a complaint increased the intention to buy again from the same shop.
json.title: Customer complaint handling and repurchase intentions

json.prompt:
You are helping a researcher build a **Boolean search query** for a systematic literature review of a broad construct that is studied under many names across fields. The query will be rendered for Scopus, Web of Science, EBSCO, ProQuest and Ovid, searched in titles and abstracts. Your task is to propose the concept blocks and the synonym terms in each block.

# The review

Research question:
- What leads employees to speak up, stay silent or report problems at work, and what follows when they do?

# Development benchmark papers

These 4 papers are known to belong in the review. They are the evidence for every proposal you make:
ground your proposals in what these papers study, how they describe it, and the words they use.

## [B1] Speaking up to supervisors: what makes service employees offer suggestions

(no abstract available)


## [B2] Why nurses keep patient-safety concerns to themselves

(no abstract available)


## [B3] Middle managers selling issues to top management

(no abstract available)


## [B4] Speaking up in the cockpit: first officers and error reporting

(no abstract available)

# Cells already defined by the researcher

construct: 'Employee voice and silence: discretionary upward communication, or its withholding, of suggestions,
  concerns and problems by employees.'
dimensions:
- name: form
  values:
  - key: voice
    label: Voice
    definition: An employee raises suggestions, concerns or proposals with someone inside the organisation who could
      act on them.
  - key: silence
    label: Silence
    definition: An employee withholds concerns, information or opinions from people who could act on them.
  - key: whistleblowing
    label: Whistleblowing
    definition: An employee reports irregularities or safety problems to an internal or external authority.
- name: focus
  values:
  - key: antecedent
    label: Antecedents
    definition: What predicts whether the behaviour occurs.
  - key: consequence
    label: Consequences
    definition: What follows for the employee, the receiver or the organisation once the behaviour has occurred.

  - B1

# The codebook's elements

question: What leads employees to speak up, stay silent or report problems upward or outward at work, and what follows
  when they do?
target_description: Empirical studies of employees who voluntarily raise suggestions, concerns or problems with
  someone who could act on them (a supervisor, senior management, an internal or external authority), or who withhold
  such input, where the study measures what predicts that behaviour or what follows from it.
elements:
- id: e1
  name: Voice, silence or reporting behaviour
  rule: The study measures employees speaking up, withholding input, or reporting problems.
  counts:
  - voice behaviour
  - speaking up
  - issue selling
  - upward communication
  - dissent
  - employee silence
  - whistleblowing
  does_not_count:
  - a climate or culture measure alone
  - a composite citizenship scale in which voice is not analysed separately
- id: e2
  name: Discretionary and directed upward or outward
  rule: The behaviour is the employee's own choice and is directed at someone who could act on it.
  counts:
  - informal suggestions to a supervisor
  - reports to a regulator or hotline
  does_not_count:
  - formal participation schemes such as works councils
  - grievance procedures as the only channel
  - sharing information with peers only
- id: e3
  name: Antecedents or consequences are studied
  rule: The study relates the behaviour to predictors, reactions or outcomes.
  counts:
  - predictors of voice or silence
  - receiver reactions
  - career, well-being or performance outcomes
  does_not_count:
  - scale development with no substantive relation tested
- id: e4
  name: Employees in work organisations
  rule: The actors are employees, members or contractors of an organisation.
  counts:
  - employees
  - nurses
  - crew members
  - students in a work placement
  does_not_count:
  - customers or consumers
  - citizens addressing government
  - patients
exclusion_reasons:
- code: a
  text: no voice, silence or reporting behaviour measured
  element: e1
- code: b
  text: not discretionary or not directed at someone who could act
  element: e2
- code: c
  text: no antecedent or consequence studied
  element: e3
- code: d
  text: actors are not employees
  element: e4
- code: e
  text: not empirical
- code: f
  text: too little information
adjacent_literatures:
- name: participation schemes and industrial democracy (works councils, codetermination)
  strains_element: e2
  decision: exclude
  reason_code: b
- name: grievance procedures as a formal channel
  strains_element: e2
  decision: maybe
  reason_code: b
  note: include when the decision to file is studied as the employee's choice
- name: organisational citizenship behaviour composites
  strains_element: e1
  decision: maybe
  reason_code: a
  note: include when voice is analysed as a separate dimension
- name: psychological safety as a climate construct
  strains_element: e1
  decision: maybe
  reason_code: a
  note: include when voice or silence is also measured
- name: customer and consumer complaining
  strains_element: e4
  decision: exclude
  reason_code: d
- name: citizen participation and political voice
  strains_element: e4
  decision: exclude
  reason_code: d
- name: peer information sharing and team communication
  strains_element: e2
  decision: exclude
  reason_code: b
checks:
- key: voice_subscale_only
  question: Is voice only one sub-dimension of a broader scale that is not analysed separately?
  if_yes: maybe
- key: formal_scheme_only
  question: Does the study examine only a formal participation scheme or procedure?
  if_yes: maybe
edge_cases:
- key: non_empirical
  case: reviews and conceptual papers on the topic
  default: maybe
- key: qualitative_only
  case: qualitative studies with no measured antecedent or outcome
  default: maybe
labels:
- group: target
  values:
  - supervisor
  - senior_management
  - external_body
  - peers
thin_abstract_rule: A record with no usable abstract is maybe unless the title alone settles it.


# What to produce

A JSON object with `blocks` and `logic`.

Each block is one concept that a relevant record must mention (role "required") or that only sharpens the search (role "optional"). Typical structure: one block per element of the construct (here: Voice, silence or reporting behaviour, Discretionary and directed upward or outward, Antecedents or consequences are studied, Employees in work organisations); where an element has distinct kinds (for example the values of the dimension "form": voice, silence, whistleblowing), one block per kind joined by OR. Three to six blocks is typical.

Each block's `terms` is a list. Write terms in this mini-language (the words below only show the syntax; take the real words from the benchmark abstracts and from the fields that study the construct):
- a word with right truncation: `behavio*`, `evaluat*`
- a quoted phrase, optionally truncated: `"decision making"`, `"team performance*"`
- a proximity group as an object: `{"near": ["employee*", "turnover"], "distance": 3}`; an inner list is an OR group: `{"near": ["effect*", ["performance", "productivity", "output"]], "distance": 5}`

Rules for terms:
- Be exhaustive within each block: the whole point of this review is that the literature uses diverse vocabulary across management, psychology, sociology, education, economics, law and the other fields that study the construct. Mine the benchmark abstracts for the words they actually use and add the terms those fields would use for the same thing. Fifty to two hundred terms per block is normal.
- Include both British and American spellings where they differ (behaviour/behavior, organisation/organization, judgement/judgment).
- Use truncation to catch inflections, but not so short that it floods (not `beha*`, yes `behavio*`).
- Use proximity for two-word concepts whose order varies ("team performance", "performance of the team").
- Do not include terms that are only about the setting or the population unless the researcher asked for them.
- Never put the whole research question in one term; each term is one concept.

`logic` combines block keys with `{"and": [...]}`, `{"or": [...]}` and `{"not": ...}`. Required blocks are joined with AND; alternative kinds with OR. Use a `not` only if the researcher's exclusion notes clearly call for one.

Add a `notes` string that explains your block design in three sentences.

glossary.definition: The share of all relevant papers the screening keeps, estimated from the validation sample's human labels; by default a paper counts as kept when the model said include or maybe. The Recall page names two others: search recall (validation seed papers the frozen search finds) and recall on independent papers (relevant papers found outside the search that it also found).
The share of the records a screening keeps that are relevant. WIDER does not report it as a headline; the recall setting named precision is something else, the planned margin.

How common relevant papers are among the records, overall or within one band. Deep in the ranking relevant papers are rare, which is why those bands need many labels before the recall bounds become narrow.
A record that belongs in the review by the codebook's criteria. For recall, relevance is what the human labels say, not what the model said.
One entry of a database export: title, abstract, authors and other details of one paper. After deduplication each paper is one unique record, and every later step works on these.
A paper you already know belongs in the review. Seed papers are split into a query development set, used to build the search, and a query validation set, kept apart to check the frozen search.
The seed papers the search strings, the concepts and the ranking may be tuned on. The model proposals and the dry run see only these papers.

The seed papers kept hidden until the search is frozen, then used to check whether the search and the ranking find them. When the search is reopened after some were shown, you choose whether they count as used, so they no longer give an independent check, or still count as validation; every output states your choice.
Marking the approved synonyms version as final so later steps use it. Freezing fixes the search you ran and opens the query validation set; the search pages call it frozen, and Unlock reopens it.
Fixing a sample. Locking fixes which records are in it, and from then on a change to a saved label in it is a correction that needs a reason, recorded in History.

Copying the frozen synonyms version into a new draft to edit it again; a locked sample is unlocked by name. An unlock is recorded in History and cannot be undone. If validation seed papers were shown before it, you choose whether they count as seen or stay validation; the choice is final and every output states it.
The text you paste into a database's search box. WIDER builds one per database from the approved synonyms, usually joining the synonyms of a concept with OR and the required concepts with AND.
One part of the research question that a record must mention to be found, such as the population or the phenomenon. Each concept gets its own list of synonyms in the search.
A word or phrase that names a concept, including spelling variants and truncated forms. The synonyms of all concepts make up the search strings.
One facet of the phenomenon the review is about. Each cell has an anchor sentence for the ranking, and the development sample draws likely includes per cell.
One sentence per cell that states the aims of a typical relevant paper, without methods or results. The ranking compares every record with these sentences.
The written criteria a record must meet to be included, element by element, with grades. The screening prompt is built from it, and every label records the codebook version it was made under.

A description of a nearby literature that looks relevant but is not. Near misses feed the development sample and the screening evaluation, where a prompt usually fails first. An adjacent literature is something else: a neighbouring field you name on its own, with its own pool in the development sample.
A record that scores high both on a cell and on a near-miss or adjacent-literature description. The development sample draws a few at random so the prompt meets the hardest decisions.

Finding records that are the same paper exported from several databases, so each paper is screened once. WIDER merges only on matching identifiers or corroborated details and leaves doubtful pairs for you to decide.

A group of similar records found by clustering the top of the ranking, described by its most distinctive terms. Clusters give the development sample topical coverage and split the comparison of configurations by area.
A list of numbers a ranking model computes from a record's title, abstract and keywords, so that similar texts get similar numbers. WIDER embeds each record once per model and keeps the result.
The order of all records by how close each one is to the anchor sentences. It sorts and never filters: every record stays in the corpus, and the samples are drawn along the ranking.

A stretch of the ranking, such as ranks 101 to 300, sampled on its own; statisticians call it a stratum, and the pages call it a band. Each band has its own sample size, so the recall estimate can give records from sparse deep bands their proper weight.
A band in which every record is labelled rather than a sample. By default the top band of the ranking is a census, so it adds no sampling uncertainty.

The records chosen on purpose to tune the screening: likely includes per cell, near misses, boundary cases, cluster examples, thin abstracts and a few clear excludes. It must be fully labelled before any model output on it is shown.
A random sample drawn band by band from the whole ranking, labelled by people and never used for tuning. The recall of the final screening is estimated on it.
A draw that takes every so many records along the ranking from a random start. WIDER draws each sampled band this way and analyses it as a simple random sample within the band.
The chance that a record of a band is drawn into the validation sample: the records sampled from the band divided by all records of the band.

How many records of its band one labelled record stands for: all records of the band divided by its labelled records. A relevant paper found deep in the ranking, where few records are sampled, counts for more.

The single best figure for recall, combining the bands with their weights. It is shown only once every sampled record has a final label, and always with its interval and the number of relevant papers it rests on.

The range of recall values that fit the labels seen, at the chosen confidence level. WIDER's primary interval is approximate and errs on the wide side; when a band shows no relevant paper it gives no interval and says why.
How often, over repeated samples, intervals made this way contain the true value. It is a protocol setting, and every interval and its label follow it.
The distance you plan for between the recall estimate and its lower bound. WIDER sets none by default; the planner uses it, if given, to compare how many labels each band needs.
The recall the screening should reach, set before any recall result is seen, together with what you will do if it is not met. The outcome is target met, target not met or inconclusive.

A recall bound that stays valid however often you look and add labels. WIDER uses these exact bounds for sampling without replacement to judge the recall target, at the price of needing more labels than a single-look interval.
One time a recall result on the validation sample is seen. Every look is recorded, so outputs can say whether a target, a change or an extension came before or after a result was seen.
A language model together with a prompt version and a temperature. Configurations are compared on the development sample, and the chosen one screens the whole corpus.
The instructions sent to the model with each record, built from the approved codebook. It asks for a grade per element with a quote from the title or abstract, and each prompt version is kept.
One reading of every record by the model, in its own call. By default two passes read each record independently, so a decision does not rest on one answer of a model that varies.
An extra pass with its own seed, made only where the first two passes disagree. Its answer settles the decision by majority.
The number of agreeing reads a decision needs. When three reads all differ there is no majority and the record becomes maybe.
The decision between include and exclude, for a label or a screening result. Maybes go on to a second screen or to a person; Unsure in deduplication is a different thing.
A person's decision on a sampled record: include, exclude or maybe, signed with the reviewer's name. Labels are the reference the model is measured against.
A person who labels records or decides what the screening left open. Every label and decision carries the reviewer's name, and one or two reviewers can label each development record.
How often two reviewers, or two model passes, gave the same decision, reported with Cohen's kappa, which corrects for agreement by chance.
The final, signed decision on a record where two reviewers disagreed, with a reason. Unadjudicated disagreements are named in every estimate and evaluation that uses them.

Hiding what could sway a decision. The labelling queue is blind by default: it shows no model output, sample or rank, and unticking Blind shows rank, band and sample, never model output; the validation seed papers stay hidden until the search is frozen; and model output on the development sample stays hidden until its labels are final.

Your yes before WIDER sends anything to a model that is not on this computer. It is asked once per model and kind of use, remembered with your name, asked again when the destination changes, and can be revoked.
Where a model runs: on this computer, on another computer of your network, or online. Only a model on this computer keeps titles and abstracts here; the others need consent.
The record of who did what and when: every change in History signed and timed, every version kept with its origin, and every model call stored. It lets a reader rebuild and audit the review.

Three things carry this word. The review protocol is the method settings in Settings and data, fingerprinted in every output; a screening protocol is one named screening run, such as "Protocol main". PRISMA item 24b asks where the plan written before the review can be read: WIDER adds the settings fingerprint, and the published protocol's location is yours to add.
The reporting guideline for systematic reviews and its flow diagram of records found, removed, screened and included. WIDER fills the diagram's counts from the project.

topics.context: The whole review in WIDER, from the question and seed papers to the search, cleaning, ranking and labelling, screening and the recall report, and how the app picks the next step.
topics.title: The WIDER procedure

topics.context: How your question and seed papers become the search strings you run in the databases, how the strings are checked against the seed papers, and why the search is frozen before it is tested.
topics.title: Building and freezing the search

topics.context: When you add seed papers before building the search, WIDER splits them into a development set that shapes the search and a validation set that tests the frozen search.
topics.title: Development and validation seed papers

topics.context: After you upload the database exports, WIDER finds records that describe the same paper, merges the sure ones and asks you about the unsure ones before ranking.
topics.title: Finding duplicate records

topics.context: After deduplication and once the anchor sentences are approved, the ranking orders every record by closeness to your question, and every sample, cluster and benchmark check is drawn from it.
topics.title: Ranking records by similarity

topics.context: After ranking, you label the screening development sample first; it is where the screening prompt is tuned on hard cases before the model screens the corpus.
topics.title: The screening development sample

topics.context: After ranking, the screening validation sample is drawn band by band from the whole ranking; its labels are what the recall estimate of screening is computed from.
topics.title: Stratified sampling for validation

topics.context: After the screening has run and every record of the validation sample (the probability sample) has a final human label, WIDER estimates what share of the relevant records the screening kept.
topics.title: The recall estimate and its interval

topics.context: Before any recall result is seen you set a recall target; at each look at the validation sample WIDER judges it as met, not met or inconclusive, and suggests how many more labels may settle it.
topics.title: The recall target and when more labels are needed

topics.context: After the screening development sample is labelled, a language model screens the title and abstract of every record, and you decide the records it leaves open on the Screening review page.
topics.title: Screening with language models

topics.context: After the samples are drawn, people label each sample record include, maybe or exclude; these labels are the reference the model is scored against and recall is estimated from.
topics.title: Human labels and agreement

topics.context: Blinding governs what a reviewer sees while labelling sample records, so that human labels are not shaped by the model's reads, the sampling design or another reviewer's decisions.
topics.title: Blinding

topics.context: Before any step sends text to a model or an online service, from building the search to screening, WIDER says what goes where and asks your consent for anything that is not on this computer.
topics.title: Consent and what leaves the computer

topics.context: Throughout the review WIDER keeps a signed history of every manual change, and at the end it builds the report, the PRISMA documents and a replication package from that record and the stored results.
topics.title: The record of the review

json.title: Reporting accounting irregularities: when do employees go to the regulator?

json.title: Soil carbon under no-till farming

json.abstract: We surveyed 380 call-centre employees about how often they told managers about recurring customer complaints. Employees passed on complaints more often when they believed managers fixed the underlying problems, and less often when their own targets were at risk.

json.abstract: Interviews with 45 nursing and engineering students on work placements asked whether they told a supervisor when they saw unsafe practice. Students spoke up when their placement supervisor had asked for feedback early on and stayed silent when they feared a poor placement grade.

json.title: Students on work placements speaking up about unsafe practice

json.abstract: We observed 35 warehouse teams and recorded how often workers warned each other about hazards on the floor. Teams with more peer warnings had fewer minor accidents. Supervisors were not involved in the warnings we recorded.

json.abstract: We analysed 8,000 ideas that employees of a utility company posted on a voluntary online suggestion platform read by managers. Employees posted more ideas after their earlier ideas received a quick reply, and ideas that were adopted led to more ideas from the same team.

json.prompt:
You are helping a researcher build a **development set** for calibrating screening. Besides true positives, the set needs *near misses*: records from literatures that are retrieved by the same search terms and look like matches, but fail one element of the codebook. To find such records in a ranked corpus, the researcher needs one reference text per near-miss literature, written in the same aims-only register as the search anchors.

# The review

Research question:
- What leads employees to speak up, stay silent or report problems at work, and what follows when they do?

# Development benchmark papers

These 4 papers are known to belong in the review. They are the evidence for every proposal you make:
ground your proposals in what these papers study, how they describe it, and the words they use.

## [B1] Speaking up to supervisors: what makes service employees offer suggestions

(no abstract available)


## [B2] Why nurses keep patient-safety concerns to themselves

(no abstract available)


## [B3] Middle managers selling issues to top management

(no abstract available)


## [B4] Speaking up in the cockpit: first officers and error reporting

(no abstract available)


# The codebook

question: What leads employees to speak up, stay silent or report problems upward or outward at work, and what follows
  when they do?
target_description: Empirical studies of employees who voluntarily raise suggestions, concerns or problems with
  someone who could act on them (a supervisor, senior management, an internal or external authority), or who withhold
  such input, where the study measures what predicts that behaviour or what follows from it.
elements:
- id: e1
  name: Voice, silence or reporting behaviour
  rule: The study measures employees speaking up, withholding input, or reporting problems.
  counts:
  - voice behaviour
  - speaking up
  - issue selling
  - upward communication
  - dissent
  - employee silence
  - whistleblowing
  does_not_count:
  - a climate or culture measure alone
  - a composite citizenship scale in which voice is not analysed separately
- id: e2
  name: Discretionary and directed upward or outward
  rule: The behaviour is the employee's own choice and is directed at someone who could act on it.
  counts:
  - informal suggestions to a supervisor
  - reports to a regulator or hotline
  does_not_count:
  - formal participation schemes such as works councils
  - grievance procedures as the only channel
  - sharing information with peers only
- id: e3
  name: Antecedents or consequences are studied
  rule: The study relates the behaviour to predictors, reactions or outcomes.
  counts:
  - predictors of voice or silence
  - receiver reactions
  - career, well-being or performance outcomes
  does_not_count:
  - scale development with no substantive relation tested
- id: e4
  name: Employees in work organisations
  rule: The actors are employees, members or contractors of an organisation.
  counts:
  - employees
  - nurses
  - crew members
  - students in a work placement
  does_not_count:
  - customers or consumers
  - citizens addressing government
  - patients
exclusion_reasons:
- code: a
  text: no voice, silence or reporting behaviour measured
  element: e1
- code: b
  text: not discretionary or not directed at someone who could act
  element: e2
- code: c
  text: no antecedent or consequence studied
  element: e3
- code: d
  text: actors are not employees
  element: e4
- code: e
  text: not empirical
- code: f
  text: too little information
adjacent_literatures:
- name: participation schemes and industrial democracy (works councils, codetermination)
  strains_element: e2
  decision: exclude
  reason_code: b
- name: grievance procedures as a formal channel
  strains_element: e2
  decision: maybe
  reason_code: b
  note: include when the decision to file is studied as the employee's choice
- name: organisational citizenship behaviour composites
  strains_element: e1
  decision: maybe
  reason_code: a
  note: include when voice is analysed as a separate dimension
- name: psychological safety as a climate construct
  strains_element: e1
  decision: maybe
  reason_code: a
  note: include when voice or silence is also measured
- name: customer and consumer complaining
  strains_element: e4
  decision: exclude
  reason_code: d
- name: citizen participation and political voice
  strains_element: e4
  decision: exclude
  reason_code: d
- name: peer information sharing and team communication
  strains_element: e2
  decision: exclude
  reason_code: b
checks:
- key: voice_subscale_only
  question: Is voice only one sub-dimension of a broader scale that is not analysed separately?
  if_yes: maybe
- key: formal_scheme_only
  question: Does the study examine only a formal participation scheme or procedure?
  if_yes: maybe
edge_cases:
- key: non_empirical
  case: reviews and conceptual papers on the topic
  default: maybe
- key: qualitative_only
  case: qualitative studies with no measured antecedent or outcome
  default: maybe
labels:
- group: target
  values:
  - supervisor
  - senior_management
  - external_body
  - peers
thin_abstract_rule: A record with no usable abstract is maybe unless the title alone settles it.

# The style of the anchors (match it)

aims only

Example anchor:

This study examines why employees withhold concerns, information or opinions from people who could act on them. We compare motives for employee silence such as fear of consequences, a sense of futility, deference and the wish to protect colleagues, and the leader behaviours and climates that strengthen or weaken them. The question is what predicts employee silence. This study examines why employees withhold concerns, information or opinions from people who could act on them. We compare motives for employee silence such as fear of consequences, a sense of futility, deference and the wish to protect colleagues, and the leader behaviours and climates that strengthen or weaken them. The question is what predicts employee silence.

# What to produce

`near_miss`: a list with one entry per adjacent literature in the codebook (and any other literature you expect the search to retrieve that fails an element). Each entry has:
- `key`: lower-case identifier
- `breaks`: the element id (e1, e2, ...) that this literature fails, or `boundary` for a literature that is included with a code
- `decision`: exclude, include or maybe, as the codebook says
- `note`: one sentence naming what is missing or different
- `text`: 90 to 150 words, one paragraph, aims-only, in the voice of a study in that literature: what it examines, what it compares, what the outcomes are, and what the question is. It must read like a plausible abstract of a study that a screener could wrongly include.

Eight to twelve entries is typical.

texts: One reviewer: the results rest on one person's labels, and their mistakes are not caught. Two independent reviewers: a second, blinded set of labels on the same records shows where the first may be wrong, and the disagreements are resolved before the results. A second reviewer is recommended for the validation includes and maybes, never required.

config.name: employee-voice
questions: What leads employees to speak up, stay silent or report problems at work, and what follows when they do?
config.title: Employee voice and silence

json.abstract: Using establishment data on 1,800 manufacturing firms, we compare productivity in firms with and without an elected works council. Firms with a works council had slightly higher productivity, mainly in larger plants.
json.title: Works councils and productivity in manufacturing firms

json.abstract: Satellite data from 2003 to 2017 show that plankton blooms started earlier in years with warmer sea-surface temperatures.
json.title: Plankton blooms and sea-surface temperature

json.abstract: We analysed 600 grievance cases that went to arbitration in unionised plants. Cases with written evidence were decided for the employee more often, and the average case took seven months.
json.authors: Hale, F.; Ivanova, G.; Jansen, H.
json.title: Grievance arbitration outcomes in unionised plants

json.abstract: Across 30 cities, neighbourhoods with more tree cover were up to three degrees cooler on summer afternoons.
json.title: Urban heat islands and tree cover

json.abstract: Across 40 firms, employees in firms with an anonymous reporting hotline said they were more willing to report problems they observed to management. The effect was strongest among employees on temporary contracts.
json.title: Anonymous hotlines and employees' willingness to report problems

json.abstract: Panel data on 96 project teams show when open disagreement with the leader helps. Team members' dissent improved the quality of team decisions when the leader explicitly asked for objections, and had no effect otherwise.
json.title: Disagreeing with the team leader in project teams

json.abstract: In a four-week diary study, 120 office employees recorded the suggestions they made and how their manager responded. A suggestion that was ignored made employees less likely to raise anything the following week.
json.title: After an ignored suggestion: do employees go quiet?

json.abstract: We measured organisational citizenship behaviour in 120 retail stores with a combined scale that covers helping colleagues, following rules and making suggestions. Stores with higher citizenship scores had higher sales the following year.
json.authors: Dalby, B.; Esposito, C.; Farrow, D.
json.title: Citizenship behaviour and team performance in retail stores

json.abstract: In a vignette experiment, 290 accountants decided how to report an irregularity they had noticed. Most chose an internal channel first. Reporting to an outside regulator became more likely when an earlier internal report had been ignored.
json.title: Reporting accounting irregularities: when do employees go to the regulator?

json.abstract: We surveyed 300 care workers about whether they raised concerns about care quality with their supervisor. Newcomers raised concerns less often than staff with longer tenure, and having an assigned mentor reduced the gap.
json.title: Newcomers and raising concerns in social care

json.abstract: A survey of 260 volunteer firefighters asked how often they told their crew commander about safety problems. Volunteers who felt their commander listened spoke up more, and those who spoke up were more likely to stay with the brigade a year later.
json.authors: Moreau, E.; Nwosu, F.; Ortega, G.
json.title: Speaking up among volunteer firefighters

json.abstract: This case description explains how a mid-sized insurer set up a programme to encourage staff to speak up, including training for managers and a monthly feedback forum. We describe the steps taken and the lessons the company drew.
json.title: Building a speak-up programme: a company's experience

json.abstract: In an online experiment, 240 business students read scenarios about a new job and said whether they would tell their manager about a problem. Students said they would speak up more often when the scenario described an open manager.
json.authors: Ortega, C.; Park, D.; Abara, E.
json.title: Would you speak up? Business students respond to workplace scenarios

json.abstract: A survey of 650 employees compared how often people working from home and in the office raised concerns with their manager. Employees working from home raised fewer concerns, but the gap closed when they had a weekly one-to-one video call.
json.authors: Bello, D.; Corvin, E.; Dalby, F.
json.title: Working from home and raising concerns with the manager

json.abstract: In 50 hospital units, a climate in which staff felt safe to take interpersonal risks went with more team learning activities and better quality ratings. Individual speaking up was not measured.
json.title: Psychological safety climate and team learning in hospital units

json.abstract: A multilevel study of 70 software teams found that team members offered more suggestions to leaders who admitted their own mistakes. Feeling safe to take interpersonal risks explained part of this link.
json.title: Humble leaders and employee suggestions in software firms

json.abstract: A study of 60 software teams spread across several countries found that teams shared more information between sites when they used a common chat tool, which shortened delivery times.
json.authors: Abara, A.; Bello, B.; Corvin, C.
json.title: Information sharing in distributed software teams

json.abstract: Using data from 18 small economies, we show how changes in central bank interest rates pass through to inflation.
json.authors: Corvin, G.; Dalby, H.; Esposito, A.
json.title: Interest rates and inflation in small open economies

json.abstract: A survey of 900 hospital patients asked whether they told staff when something about their care seemed wrong. Patients who had been invited to ask questions on admission raised concerns more often.
json.title: Patients raising concerns with hospital staff

json.abstract: We studied how union representatives in 30 workplaces put members' complaints on the agenda of formal consultation meetings with management. Complaints raised in writing before the meeting were resolved more often.
json.title: Union representatives raising members' complaints in formal meetings

json.abstract: In a two-wave survey of 540 school teachers, those who often kept concerns from their head teacher reported more emotional exhaustion a year later. The link held after accounting for workload.
json.title: The cost of silence: withheld concerns and exhaustion among teachers

json.abstract: We developed a six-item scale of how often employees make suggestions at work and tested it in two samples of 300 and 450 employees. The items formed one factor, and scores correlated moderately with job satisfaction, which we report as evidence of validity.
json.title: A short scale for measuring employee suggestions

json.abstract: We studied 25 towns that let residents vote on part of the municipal budget. Turnout was higher where the town held neighbourhood meetings before the vote.
json.title: Citizen participation in municipal budgeting

json.abstract: Field trials over ten years found more carbon in the top soil layer of fields farmed without ploughing.
json.title: Soil carbon under no-till farming

json.abstract: We surveyed 380 call-centre employees about how often they told managers about recurring customer complaints. Employees passed on complaints more often when they believed managers fixed the underlying problems, and less often when their own targets were at risk.
json.title: Front-line staff passing customer complaints on to managers

json.abstract: Interviews with 45 nursing and engineering students on work placements asked whether they told a supervisor when they saw unsafe practice. Students spoke up when their placement supervisor had asked for feedback early on and stayed silent when they feared a poor placement grade.
json.authors: Kowal, G.; Lindqvist, H.; Moreau, A.
json.title: Students on work placements speaking up about unsafe practice

json.abstract: Hospital pharmacists must report every dispensing incident to a national system. Using five years of records from 22 hospitals, we found that report numbers rose after the system was simplified, and that hospitals with more reports had fewer repeated incidents.
json.title: Mandatory incident reporting by hospital pharmacists

json.abstract: We report a catalyst that produces ammonia at lower pressure than current methods and test it over 500 hours.
json.authors: Jansen, D.; Kowal, E.; Lindqvist, F.
json.title: A new catalyst for ammonia production

json.abstract: We observed 35 warehouse teams and recorded how often workers warned each other about hazards on the floor. Teams with more peer warnings had fewer minor accidents. Supervisors were not involved in the warnings we recorded.
json.title: Warning colleagues about hazards in warehouse teams

json.abstract: Observers recorded how often team members in 48 surgical teams pointed out possible errors during operations. Team members spoke up more often in teams whose surgeon had introduced everyone by name at the start, and errors were caught earlier in those teams.
json.title: Speaking up about errors in surgical teams

json.abstract: We analysed 8,000 ideas that employees of a utility company posted on a voluntary online suggestion platform read by managers. Employees posted more ideas after their earlier ideas received a quick reply, and ideas that were adopted led to more ideas from the same team.
json.authors: Farrow, H.; Gunnarsdottir, A.; Hale, B.
json.title: Employee ideas on an online suggestion platform

json.abstract: An online survey of 1,100 shoppers found that a quick and friendly response to a complaint increased the intention to buy again from the same shop.
json.title: Customer complaint handling and repurchase intentions

json.keep_before: Samples keep the version they were drawn from: validation and development keep version 1.

rows.title: Front-line staff passing customer complaints on to managers

anchors.silence_consequence: This study examines what follows when employees stay silent about problems, errors or ideas: effects on the individual's stress, engagement and intention to leave, and on the team's error detection, learning and performance. We compare individual, leader and climate predictors of promotive and prohibitive voice, issue selling and upward communication, measured through surveys, diaries and vignettes. The question is which conditions make employees more likely to raise issues upward. The question is which conditions make employees more likely to raise issues upward.
anchors.voice_consequence: This study examines what happens after employees speak up: how supervisors and senior managers react to suggestions, concerns and proposals, and what follows for the speaker's performance ratings, reputation, career and well-being, and for the unit's decisions and improvement. We compare individual, situational and organisational predictors of whistleblowing intentions and actual reporting, including channel choice and anonymity. The question is which conditions make reporting more likely. We compare individual, situational and organisational predictors of whistleblowing intentions and actual reporting, including channel choice and anonymity. The question is which conditions make reporting more likely.
anchors.whistleblowing_consequence: This study examines what happens to employees after they report irregularities or safety problems to an internal or external authority: retaliation, career outcomes, well-being and the organisational response to the report, as well as whether the problem was corrected. We compare reporters who used different channels. The question is what the consequences of whistleblowing are.
