json.abstract: Using establishment data on 1,800 manufacturing firms, we compare productivity in firms with and without an elected works council. Firms with a works council had slightly higher productivity, mainly in larger plants.
json.title: Works councils and productivity in manufacturing firms

json.abstract: Satellite data from 2003 to 2017 show that plankton blooms started earlier in years with warmer sea-surface temperatures.
json.title: Plankton blooms and sea-surface temperature

json.abstract: We analysed 600 grievance cases that went to arbitration in unionised plants. Cases with written evidence were decided for the employee more often, and the average case took seven months.
json.authors: Hale, F.; Ivanova, G.; Jansen, H.
json.title: Grievance arbitration outcomes in unionised plants

json.abstract: Across 30 cities, neighbourhoods with more tree cover were up to three degrees cooler on summer afternoons.
json.title: Urban heat islands and tree cover

json.abstract: Across 40 firms, employees in firms with an anonymous reporting hotline said they were more willing to report problems they observed to management. The effect was strongest among employees on temporary contracts.
json.title: Anonymous hotlines and employees' willingness to report problems

json.abstract: Panel data on 96 project teams show when open disagreement with the leader helps. Team members' dissent improved the quality of team decisions when the leader explicitly asked for objections, and had no effect otherwise.
json.title: Disagreeing with the team leader in project teams

json.abstract: In a four-week diary study, 120 office employees recorded the suggestions they made and how their manager responded. A suggestion that was ignored made employees less likely to raise anything the following week.
json.title: After an ignored suggestion: do employees go quiet?

json.abstract: We measured organisational citizenship behaviour in 120 retail stores with a combined scale that covers helping colleagues, following rules and making suggestions. Stores with higher citizenship scores had higher sales the following year.
json.authors: Dalby, B.; Esposito, C.; Farrow, D.
json.title: Citizenship behaviour and team performance in retail stores

json.abstract: In a vignette experiment, 290 accountants decided how to report an irregularity they had noticed. Most chose an internal channel first. Reporting to an outside regulator became more likely when an earlier internal report had been ignored.
json.title: Reporting accounting irregularities: when do employees go to the regulator?

json.abstract: We surveyed 300 care workers about whether they raised concerns about care quality with their supervisor. Newcomers raised concerns less often than staff with longer tenure, and having an assigned mentor reduced the gap.
json.title: Newcomers and raising concerns in social care

json.abstract: A survey of 260 volunteer firefighters asked how often they told their crew commander about safety problems. Volunteers who felt their commander listened spoke up more, and those who spoke up were more likely to stay with the brigade a year later.
json.authors: Moreau, E.; Nwosu, F.; Ortega, G.
json.title: Speaking up among volunteer firefighters

json.abstract: This case description explains how a mid-sized insurer set up a programme to encourage staff to speak up, including training for managers and a monthly feedback forum. We describe the steps taken and the lessons the company drew.
json.title: Building a speak-up programme: a company's experience

json.abstract: In an online experiment, 240 business students read scenarios about a new job and said whether they would tell their manager about a problem. Students said they would speak up more often when the scenario described an open manager.
json.authors: Ortega, C.; Park, D.; Abara, E.
json.title: Would you speak up? Business students respond to workplace scenarios

json.abstract: A survey of 650 employees compared how often people working from home and in the office raised concerns with their manager. Employees working from home raised fewer concerns, but the gap closed when they had a weekly one-to-one video call.
json.authors: Bello, D.; Corvin, E.; Dalby, F.
json.title: Working from home and raising concerns with the manager

json.abstract: In 50 hospital units, a climate in which staff felt safe to take interpersonal risks went with more team learning activities and better quality ratings. Individual speaking up was not measured.
json.title: Psychological safety climate and team learning in hospital units

json.abstract: A multilevel study of 70 software teams found that team members offered more suggestions to leaders who admitted their own mistakes. Feeling safe to take interpersonal risks explained part of this link.
json.title: Humble leaders and employee suggestions in software firms

json.abstract: A study of 60 software teams spread across several countries found that teams shared more information between sites when they used a common chat tool, which shortened delivery times.
json.authors: Abara, A.; Bello, B.; Corvin, C.
json.title: Information sharing in distributed software teams

json.abstract: Using data from 18 small economies, we show how changes in central bank interest rates pass through to inflation.
json.authors: Corvin, G.; Dalby, H.; Esposito, A.
json.title: Interest rates and inflation in small open economies

json.abstract: A survey of 900 hospital patients asked whether they told staff when something about their care seemed wrong. Patients who had been invited to ask questions on admission raised concerns more often.
json.title: Patients raising concerns with hospital staff

json.abstract: We studied how union representatives in 30 workplaces put members' complaints on the agenda of formal consultation meetings with management. Complaints raised in writing before the meeting were resolved more often.
json.title: Union representatives raising members' complaints in formal meetings

json.abstract: In a two-wave survey of 540 school teachers, those who often kept concerns from their head teacher reported more emotional exhaustion a year later. The link held after accounting for workload.
json.title: The cost of silence: withheld concerns and exhaustion among teachers

json.abstract: We developed a six-item scale of how often employees make suggestions at work and tested it in two samples of 300 and 450 employees. The items formed one factor, and scores correlated moderately with job satisfaction, which we report as evidence of validity.
json.title: A short scale for measuring employee suggestions

json.abstract: We studied 25 towns that let residents vote on part of the municipal budget. Turnout was higher where the town held neighbourhood meetings before the vote.
json.title: Citizen participation in municipal budgeting

json.abstract: Field trials over ten years found more carbon in the top soil layer of fields farmed without ploughing.
json.title: Soil carbon under no-till farming

json.abstract: We surveyed 380 call-centre employees about how often they told managers about recurring customer complaints. Employees passed on complaints more often when they believed managers fixed the underlying problems, and less often when their own targets were at risk.
json.title: Front-line staff passing customer complaints on to managers

json.abstract: Interviews with 45 nursing and engineering students on work placements asked whether they told a supervisor when they saw unsafe practice. Students spoke up when their placement supervisor had asked for feedback early on and stayed silent when they feared a poor placement grade.
json.authors: Kowal, G.; Lindqvist, H.; Moreau, A.
json.title: Students on work placements speaking up about unsafe practice

json.abstract: Hospital pharmacists must report every dispensing incident to a national system. Using five years of records from 22 hospitals, we found that report numbers rose after the system was simplified, and that hospitals with more reports had fewer repeated incidents.
json.title: Mandatory incident reporting by hospital pharmacists

json.abstract: We report a catalyst that produces ammonia at lower pressure than current methods and test it over 500 hours.
json.authors: Jansen, D.; Kowal, E.; Lindqvist, F.
json.title: A new catalyst for ammonia production

json.abstract: We observed 35 warehouse teams and recorded how often workers warned each other about hazards on the floor. Teams with more peer warnings had fewer minor accidents. Supervisors were not involved in the warnings we recorded.
json.title: Warning colleagues about hazards in warehouse teams

json.abstract: Observers recorded how often team members in 48 surgical teams pointed out possible errors during operations. Team members spoke up more often in teams whose surgeon had introduced everyone by name at the start, and errors were caught earlier in those teams.
json.title: Speaking up about errors in surgical teams

json.abstract: We analysed 8,000 ideas that employees of a utility company posted on a voluntary online suggestion platform read by managers. Employees posted more ideas after their earlier ideas received a quick reply, and ideas that were adopted led to more ideas from the same team.
json.authors: Farrow, H.; Gunnarsdottir, A.; Hale, B.
json.title: Employee ideas on an online suggestion platform

json.abstract: An online survey of 1,100 shoppers found that a quick and friendly response to a complaint increased the intention to buy again from the same shop.
json.title: Customer complaint handling and repurchase intentions

record.abstract: Interviews with 45 nursing and engineering students on work placements asked whether they told a supervisor when they saw unsafe practice. Students spoke up when their placement supervisor had asked for feedback early on and stayed silent when they feared a poor placement grade.
record.authors: Kowal, G.; Lindqvist, H.; Moreau, A.
record.title: Students on work placements speaking up about unsafe practice

queue.title_b: Reporting accounting irregularities: when do employees go to the regulator?

queue.title_b: Speaking up in the cockpit: first officers and error reporting

queue.abstract_b: In a four-week diary study, 120 office employees recorded the suggestions they made and how their manager responded. A suggestion that was ignored made employees less likely to raise anything the following week.

queue.title_b: After an ignored suggestion: do employees go quiet?

queue.title_b: Newcomers and raising concerns in social care

queue.abstract_b: Across 40 firms, employees in firms with an anonymous reporting hotline said they were more willing to report problems they observed to management. The effect was strongest among employees on temporary contracts.

queue.title_b: Anonymous hotlines and employees' willingness to report problems

queue.abstract_b: We developed a six-item scale of how often employees make suggestions at work and tested it in two samples of 300 and 450 employees. The items formed one factor, and scores correlated moderately with job satisfaction, which we report as evidence of validity.

queue.title_b: A short scale for measuring employee suggestions

queue.abstract_b: Hospital pharmacists must report every dispensing incident to a national system. Using five years of records from 22 hospitals, we found that report numbers rose after the system was simplified, and that hospitals with more reports had fewer repeated incidents.

queue.title_b: Mandatory incident reporting by hospital pharmacists

json.prompt:
You are helping a researcher set up a systematic literature review of a broad construct that is studied under many names across fields. Your task now is to propose the **cells** of the construct: the small number of dimensions whose combinations partition the literature, so that the review can check it covers every combination and can write one search anchor per cell.

# The review

Research question:
- What leads employees to speak up, stay silent or report problems at work, and what follows when they do?

# Development benchmark papers

These 4 papers are known to belong in the review. They are the evidence for every proposal you make:
ground your proposals in what these papers study, how they describe it, and the words they use.

## [B1] Speaking up to supervisors: what makes service employees offer suggestions

(no abstract available)


## [B2] Why nurses keep patient-safety concerns to themselves

(no abstract available)


## [B3] Middle managers selling issues to top management

(no abstract available)


## [B4] Speaking up in the cockpit: first officers and error reporting

(no abstract available)


# What to produce

1. A one-sentence statement of the construct.
2. One to three dimensions. Each dimension has two to five mutually exclusive values with a key (lower-case identifier), a label and a one-sentence definition. Choose dimensions that (a) every benchmark paper can be placed on, (b) separate literatures that use different vocabulary, and (c) matter for the research question. Good dimensions are *kinds of the focal phenomenon* (the kind of behaviour, event or practice the study is about) and *kinds of outcome or response* (what the study measures). Do not use as a dimension: the variable whose effect the question asks about (its levels are not literatures but conditions inside every study), moderators such as role or context, the setting (for example workplace, school, online), the population, or the method.
3. The cells: every combination of the dimension values that could plausibly contain studies. For each cell give a key (join the value keys with an underscore), its labels (dimension name → value key), one sentence stating what a study in this cell asks, and the benchmark ids that belong to it (a paper may appear in more than one cell; list the main one first).
4. `not_a_criterion`: things that might look like dimensions but should not restrict eligibility (for example setting, population, method).

Keep definitions in plain language. Prefer fewer cells over more; eight is typical, sixteen is the maximum.

data.prompt:
You are screening one bibliographic record, by title and abstract only, for a systematic review. Decide whether the record could belong in the review.

# How to work

- Judge only from the title and abstract supplied. Do not use anything you may know about the paper, its authors or its journal. Never invent detail that is not in the text.
- Check the four elements one by one, answer the two checks, compare the study with the paper we are looking for, then decide.
- For every element, quote the words of the text that support your grade, verbatim. A quote is a copy of words from the title or abstract, never a sentence of your own: do not write "The abstract does not mention ..." in a quote field. A grade of "absent" is allowed only with a copied quote of the words that show the element is missing. If you cannot copy such words, leave the quote "" and grade "unclear".
- A wrong exclusion is lost for good; a wrong inclusion costs one full-text read. Exclude only when the study is unrelated to the topic or when you have quoted the words that show an element is absent. In every other case of doubt, choose "maybe" and say what is missing.
- A record with no usable abstract is maybe unless the title alone settles it.

# The paper we are looking for

Empirical studies of employees who voluntarily raise suggestions, concerns or problems with someone who could act on them (a supervisor, senior management, an internal or external authority), or who withhold such input, where the study measures what predicts that behaviour or what follows from it.

# The question

What leads employees to speak up, stay silent or report problems upward or outward at work, and what follows when they do?

# The four elements

A record is eligible when all four elements are plausibly present.

1. Voice, silence or reporting behaviour. The study measures employees speaking up, withholding input, or reporting problems. Counts: voice behaviour; speaking up; issue selling; upward communication; dissent; employee silence; whistleblowing. Does not count: a climate or culture measure alone; a composite citizenship scale in which voice is not analysed separately.2. Discretionary and directed upward or outward. The behaviour is the employee's own choice and is directed at someone who could act on it. Counts: informal suggestions to a supervisor; reports to a regulator or hotline. Does not count: formal participation schemes such as works councils; grievance procedures as the only channel; sharing information with peers only.3. Antecedents or consequences are studied. The study relates the behaviour to predictors, reactions or outcomes. Counts: predictors of voice or silence; receiver reactions; career, well-being or performance outcomes. Does not count: scale development with no substantive relation tested.4. Employees in work organisations. The actors are employees, members or contractors of an organisation. Counts: employees; nurses; crew members; students in a work placement. Does not count: customers or consumers; citizens addressing government; patients.Not a criterion: setting or industry; occupation; country; research method.

# Two checks, decided by the review author, that you must answer before deciding

1. voice_subscale_only. Is voice only one sub-dimension of a broader scale that is not analysed separately? If yes: maybe
2. formal_scheme_only. Does the study examine only a formal participation scheme or procedure? If yes: maybe

# Adjacent literatures that look like includes but are not

- participation schemes and industrial democracy (works councils, codetermination) (strains e2): exclude, reason b- grievance procedures as a formal channel (strains e2): maybe, reason b. include when the decision to file is studied as the employee's choice- organisational citizenship behaviour composites (strains e1): maybe, reason a. include when voice is analysed as a separate dimension- psychological safety as a climate construct (strains e1): maybe, reason a. include when voice or silence is also measured- customer and consumer complaining (strains e4): exclude, reason d- citizen participation and political voice (strains e4): exclude, reason d- peer information sharing and team communication (strains e2): exclude, reason b
# Edge cases, decided by the review author

- reviews and conceptual papers on the topic: maybe (edge_case "non_empirical")
- qualitative studies with no measured antecedent or outcome: maybe (edge_case "qualitative_only")

# The cells

If the record is an include, name the cell that fits its main question.

- voice_antecedent: what leads employees to speak up with suggestions or concerns
- voice_consequence: how receivers react to voice and what follows for the speaker
- silence_antecedent: why employees withhold concerns or opinions
- silence_consequence: what follows when employees stay silent
- whistleblowing_antecedent: what leads employees to report irregularities to an authority
- whistleblowing_consequence: what happens to employees after they report irregularities

# Decision

- include: all four elements are plausibly present from the title and abstract.
- exclude: only when the study is unrelated to the topic, or when you have graded an element absent with a quote of the words that show it. Give one reason: a, no voice, silence or reporting behaviour measured; b, not discretionary or not directed at someone who could act; c, no antecedent or consequence studied; d, actors are not employees; e, not empirical; f, too little information.- maybe: in every other case: you cannot tell from the text, a check says so, an edge case applies, the paper is non-empirical but on topic, or there is no usable abstract. Say what is missing.

# Output

Return only one JSON object with exactly these fields, in this order:

- summary: one sentence in your own words saying what the study did and what it compared. Not the title.
- e1: "present", "unclear" or "absent" for voice, silence or reporting behaviour.
- e1_quote: the words of the text your grade rests on, copied verbatim, or "" if none.
- e2: "present", "unclear" or "absent" for discretionary and directed upward or outward.
- e2_quote: the words of the text your grade rests on, copied verbatim, or "" if none.
- e3: "present", "unclear" or "absent" for antecedents or consequences are studied.
- e3_quote: the words of the text your grade rests on, copied verbatim, or "" if none.
- e4: "present", "unclear" or "absent" for employees in work organisations.
- e4_quote: the words of the text your grade rests on, copied verbatim, or "" if none.
- voice_subscale_only: true or false.
- formal_scheme_only: true or false.
- target_fit: "core" if this is the kind of study described above; "adjacent" if it is about the topic but an element is missing or unclear; "unrelated" if it is about neither.
- edge_case: "non_empirical", "qualitative_only" or "none".
- decision: "include", "maybe" or "exclude".
- exclusion_reason: "a", "b", "c", "d", "e", "f", or "none".
- missing_for_maybe: for a maybe, what the text does not say; otherwise "".
- cell: for an include, one of "voice_antecedent", "voice_consequence", "silence_antecedent", "silence_consequence", "whistleblowing_antecedent", "whistleblowing_consequence"; otherwise "not_applicable".
- target: for an include, one of "supervisor", "senior_management", "external_body", "peers"; otherwise "not_applicable".

json.draft: We searched alpha, beta and gamma (exports imported 2026-10-20) with a Boolean query (synonym blocks version 1, frozen), developed against 4 known-relevant development papers and tested once on 2 held-out validation papers. Seed papers were split into a development set and a validation set. Where the validation papers came from: 2 added by the researcher. Recall on the validation set: 2 of 2, 95% interval 0.16 to 1.00. 2 validation papers were also found by the query. The searches returned 74 records; deduplication by DOI, exact title and corroborated fuzzy title matching, with 11 uncertain pairs decided by hand left 39 unique records. Records were ranked by their similarity to one anchor sentence per construct cell (anchors version 1, mean of the top 2 cells) using the embedding model BAAI/bge-m3. The procedure, prompts, run specifications and all numbers are reproducible from the project with WIDER (protocol hash 19f81d9dcb7a).

Band S3 shows no relevant paper in 3 labelled records of 3; it may still hold up to 0 relevant papers (exact bound).

Exact bounds valid at every look (95%): the relevant records of each band's kept and not-kept records are bounded with a confidence sequence for sampling without replacement (Waudby-Smith and Ramdas 2020), the error split equally over the 6 cells; the guarantee holds per result set and recall variant, whatever is added between looks.
The first draw is systematic and is treated as random within each band.

The bounds are conservative: the error is split over every band and screening decision and each is bounded on its own, so they may need substantially more labels than a sharper method to show the same result.
Band S2 (8 records not kept, 0 of 5 relevant) leaves up to 3 relevant papers unseen; its share of the bound is 100%.

11 records of the development sample were drawn after validation; its estimate and bounds count them as records of their bands that validation did not label.

json.prompt:
You are helping a researcher rank a large corpus of titles and abstracts by similarity to the studies they are looking for. The ranking uses one **anchor text** per cell: a paragraph written as if it were the aims section of the ideal study in that cell. Records are scored by cosine similarity between their title+abstract and each anchor, so the anchor must read like an abstract's aims, in the same register as real abstracts.

# The review

Research question:
- What leads employees to speak up, stay silent or report problems at work, and what follows when they do?

# Development benchmark papers

These 4 papers are known to belong in the review. They are the evidence for every proposal you make:
ground your proposals in what these papers study, how they describe it, and the words they use.

## [B1] Speaking up to supervisors: what makes service employees offer suggestions

(no abstract available)


## [B2] Why nurses keep patient-safety concerns to themselves

(no abstract available)


## [B3] Middle managers selling issues to top management

(no abstract available)


## [B4] Speaking up in the cockpit: first officers and error reporting

(no abstract available)


# The cells

construct: 'Employee voice and silence: discretionary upward communication, or its withholding, of suggestions,
  concerns and problems by employees.'
dimensions:
- name: form
  values:
  - key: voice
    label: Voice
    definition: An employee raises suggestions, concerns or proposals with someone inside the organisation who could
      act on them.
  - key: silence
    label: Silence
    definition: An employee withholds concerns, information or opinions from people who could act on them.
  - key: whistleblowing
    label: Whistleblowing
    definition: An employee reports irregularities or safety problems to an internal or external authority.
- name: focus
  values:
  - key: antecedent
    label: Antecedents
    definition: What predicts whether the behaviour occurs.
  - key: consequence
    label: Consequences
    definition: What follows for the employee, the receiver or the organisation once the behaviour has occurred.
cells:
- key: voice_antecedent
  labels:
    form: voice
    focus: antecedent
  question: what leads employees to speak up with suggestions or concerns
  benchmark_ids:
  - B1
- key: voice_consequence
  labels:
    form: voice
    focus: consequence
  question: how receivers react to voice and what follows for the speaker
  benchmark_ids:
  - B4
  - B5
- key: silence_antecedent
  labels:
    form: silence
    focus: antecedent
  question: why employees withhold concerns or opinions
  benchmark_ids:
  - B2
- key: silence_consequence
  labels:
    form: silence
    focus: consequence
  question: what follows when employees stay silent
- key: whistleblowing_antecedent
  labels:
    form: whistleblowing
    focus: antecedent
  question: what leads employees to report irregularities to an authority
  benchmark_ids:
  - B3
- key: whistleblowing_consequence
  labels:
    form: whistleblowing
    focus: consequence
  question: what happens to employees after they report irregularities
  benchmark_ids:
  - B6
not_a_criterion:
- setting or industry
- occupation
- country
- research method


# What to produce

Write an anchor for each of these cells: voice_antecedent, voice_consequence, silence_antecedent, silence_consequence, whistleblowing_antecedent, whistleblowing_consequence, as `anchors: {cell_key: text}`.

Rules for every anchor:
- 180 to 260 words, one paragraph, present tense, the voice of a study describing its own aims ("This study examines whether...", "We compare...").
- Aims only: no results, no findings, no numbers, no theory names, no citations, no method details beyond the comparison being made.
- State the comparison the cell is about, who the actors are, who else is involved, and name the outcomes the cell covers with several concrete variants (the diverse words the literature uses), because those words are what the similarity will pick up.
- Mention several concrete instances of the focal phenomenon (the kinds that the cell's dimension values name, in the words the benchmark abstracts use) in the same way a real abstract would.
- Say what the question is in the last sentence.
- Do not mention the setting unless the cell is about setting. Do not list exclusions; the anchor describes what we want, not what we do not.
- The anchors for different cells must differ in the outcome words and the words for the focal phenomenon, not just in one phrase.
Also return `style`: one sentence describing the register you used, so later anchors can match it.

json.route: The search strings are frozen; the records come from the searches they record. Seed paper coverage is checked once the query is frozen or the uploads are marked final.

stages.description: Write down the research question(s), the inclusion and exclusion notes, the seed papers (a development and a validation set), and the databases you will search. Everything later is checked against these inputs.
stages.title: Review plan
stages.why: A review of a broad construct drifts unless the question and the known-relevant papers are fixed first; the validation seed papers are held back so the search can be tested once, honestly.

stages.description: The LLM proposes, from your question and the development seed papers' abstracts, the construct cells, the screening codebook, synonym blocks for the query, one anchor sentence per cell, and near-miss (adjacent literature) descriptions. You edit and approve each; every version is kept.
stages.title: Concepts and synonyms
stages.why: Broad constructs are reviewed well only when their vocabulary and boundaries are written down before searching; grounding the proposals in your own seed papers keeps them specific to your literature.

stages.description: The approved synonym blocks are rendered into one Boolean string per chosen database, in that database's own syntax. You run the searches yourself and bring back the exports. Coverage of the development seed papers is checked while you edit; the validation set is reported only once the query is frozen or the uploads are marked final.
stages.title: Search strings
stages.why: Databases differ in syntax and limits; one shared query representation keeps the strings consistent and reproducible, and the freeze rule prevents tuning the query to the test papers.

stages.description: Database exports (RIS, CSV/TSV, XLS/XLSX or BibTeX, one folder per database) are recognised by their header, standardised and stored with their source file; a file is imported once, by content hash, and gets a sanity verdict (ok, capped, off-topic, empty, duplicate). Coverage then shows which seed papers each database returned (by DOI, exact title, then fuzzy title) and, after dedup, which the corpus holds.
stages.title: Search results
stages.why: An export that is not the result of your query (wrong search, truncated download) silently ruins recall; a seed paper missing from the database that should have found it is the cheapest warning you will get.

stages.description: Records are merged by DOI, then exact title, then fuzzy title with corroboration (year, first author, journal). Uncertain pairs go to a manual queue; your decisions are stored and re-applied. PRISMA counts and audit files are written.
stages.title: Deduplication
stages.why: Rules alone over-merge or under-merge; a transparent queue with named rules makes the counts auditable.

stages.description: Records with a thin or missing abstract are completed from OpenAlex, Crossref, Europe PMC and Semantic Scholar in that order; nothing already present is overwritten and every fetch is logged.
stages.title: Missing abstracts
stages.why: Ranking and screening read the abstract; a record without one is judged on its title alone, so it is easily ranked low or set aside.

stages.description: Every record is embedded and scored against the approved anchors (mean of its top cells). The ranking sorts, never filters. Seed-paper ranks, recall@K and tests without one part over anchor versions and embedding models show how well the anchors work; clusters in the top of the ranking describe the topics found.
stages.title: Ranking
stages.why: A ranking lets the human and LLM effort concentrate where relevant papers are dense, while a probability sample over the whole ranking keeps the recall estimate honest.

stages.description: A band-stratified probability sample (for the recall estimate) and a purposive development set (likely includes, near-misses per adjacent literature, cluster medoids, thin abstracts, tail) are drawn and labelled in the blinded queue by one or two reviewers.
stages.title: Samples and labelling
stages.why: Human labels on a known design are what make the LLM's recall measurable; the development set is where the prompt is tuned on the hardest cases.

stages.description: The codebook becomes a prompt and JSON schema; each record is screened in an isolated call that quotes the words behind every grade, and an "absent" grade whose quote is not in the record becomes unclear. Development-set evaluation reports misses per adjacent literature; the corpus protocol runs two passes, a blind third read on disagreement and a second screen of the maybes.
stages.title: Screening
stages.why: Verbatim quotes and a recall-first rule keep a small model from excluding on a hunch; repeated reads and a blind third read on disagreement catch some of its slips, and show where it answers inconsistently.

stages.description: Band-weighted recall of the LLM screen against the human labels, with an interval and the number of relevant papers, the PRISMA flow and a shareable report without abstracts.
stages.title: Recall and report
stages.why: The claim a review makes is "we found nearly all of it"; this stage puts a number and an interval on it.

stages.description: Stage-2 extension point.
stages.title: Full-text screening
stages.why: Abstract-level screening leaves the includes and maybes; reading their full texts is the next decision layer.

stages.description: Stage-2 extension point.
stages.title: Data extraction
stages.why: Once the set is final, the same codebook elements can be extracted per paper for the synthesis.

stages.description: Stage-2 extension point.
stages.title: Synthesis
stages.why: The extracted elements are what a synthesis of a wide literature is built from.

json.draft: We searched alpha, beta and gamma (exports imported 2026-10-20) with a Boolean query (synonym blocks version 1, frozen), developed against 4 known-relevant development papers and tested once on 2 held-out validation papers. Seed papers were split into a development set and a validation set. Where the validation papers came from: 2 added by the researcher. Recall on the validation set: 2 of 2, 95% interval 0.16 to 1.00. 2 validation papers were also found by the query. The searches returned 74 records; deduplication by DOI, exact title and corroborated fuzzy title matching, with 11 uncertain pairs decided by hand left 39 unique records. Records were ranked by their similarity to one anchor sentence per construct cell (anchors version 1, mean of the top 2 cells) using the embedding model BAAI/bge-m3. A band-stratified probability sample of 16 records across the ranking and a purposive development set of 16 records were labelled by 1 reviewer. Each development sample record needed one reviewer's final label. Titles and abstracts were screened by gpt-4o-mini against a codebook of 4 elements; every grade had to be supported by a verbatim quote, and a record was excluded only when the construct was shown to be absent or the study unrelated. Two independent reads with a blind third read on disagreement were combined by a 2-of-3 majority (protocol main set 2): 18 records were included and 4 kept for full-text reading, of 39 screened. Every pass (pass A, pass B and the judge) used gpt-4o-mini. Passes A, B and the judge use the same model (gpt-4o-mini, temperature 0.7): their readings are not independent. Against the human labels of the probability sample, the band-weighted recall of the screening (lenient variant) was 1.00 (95% interval 0.54 to 1.00, Kish effective size method; 7 relevant validation papers). Recall on validation was seen for 2 result sets with different settings (sets 1, 2); choosing between them on this sample uses it for model selection. No recall target was set in advance. The first draw is systematic and is treated as random within each band; the guarantee at every look assumes a random draw (an open question). The bounds are conservative: the error is split over every band and screening decision and each is bounded on its own, so they may need substantially more labels than a sharper method to show the same result. This estimate covers 27 ranked records (not the 6 records with too short an abstract, or the 6 seed papers), screened on title and abstract only; it says nothing about full-text screening. No independent second review was done; one reviewer labelled the samples. The procedure, prompts, run specifications and all numbers are reproducible from the project with WIDER (protocol hash 19f81d9dcb7a).

items: Section 2, Data cleaning: Deduplication, step 1 of 2 in this section (needs attention: 11 pairs to decide).

parts.heading: What to do
items: Check the list of uploads: every database you searched should be there.
Press Run deduplication (after the first run this button reads Apply decisions and check again).

Some pairs look alike but WIDER is not sure. Decide each one: Duplicates, keep A or Duplicates, keep B (the kept record's title, authors, year, journal and DOI stand for the paper), Not duplicates or Unsure.
Press Apply decisions and check again to apply your decisions.

parts.heading: Why it matters
items: The same paper often comes back from several databases. This step finds those duplicates so each paper is screened once, and the PRISMA counts of records found and removed are final once every pair is decided and the decisions are applied.

json.route: The search strings are frozen; the records come from the searches they record. Seed paper coverage is checked once the query is frozen or the uploads are marked final.

stages.description: Write down the research question(s), the inclusion and exclusion notes, the seed papers (a development and a validation set), and the databases you will search. Everything later is checked against these inputs.
stages.title: Review plan
stages.why: A review of a broad construct drifts unless the question and the known-relevant papers are fixed first; the validation seed papers are held back so the search can be tested once, honestly.

stages.description: The LLM proposes, from your question and the development seed papers' abstracts, the construct cells, the screening codebook, synonym blocks for the query, one anchor sentence per cell, and near-miss (adjacent literature) descriptions. You edit and approve each; every version is kept.
stages.title: Concepts and synonyms
stages.why: Broad constructs are reviewed well only when their vocabulary and boundaries are written down before searching; grounding the proposals in your own seed papers keeps them specific to your literature.

stages.description: The approved synonym blocks are rendered into one Boolean string per chosen database, in that database's own syntax. You run the searches yourself and bring back the exports. Coverage of the development seed papers is checked while you edit; the validation set is reported only once the query is frozen or the uploads are marked final.
stages.title: Search strings
stages.why: Databases differ in syntax and limits; one shared query representation keeps the strings consistent and reproducible, and the freeze rule prevents tuning the query to the test papers.

stages.description: Database exports (RIS, CSV/TSV, XLS/XLSX or BibTeX, one folder per database) are recognised by their header, standardised and stored with their source file; a file is imported once, by content hash, and gets a sanity verdict (ok, capped, off-topic, empty, duplicate). Coverage then shows which seed papers each database returned (by DOI, exact title, then fuzzy title) and, after dedup, which the corpus holds.
stages.title: Search results
stages.why: An export that is not the result of your query (wrong search, truncated download) silently ruins recall; a seed paper missing from the database that should have found it is the cheapest warning you will get.

stages.description: Records are merged by DOI, then exact title, then fuzzy title with corroboration (year, first author, journal). Uncertain pairs go to a manual queue; your decisions are stored and re-applied. PRISMA counts and audit files are written.
stages.title: Deduplication
stages.why: Rules alone over-merge or under-merge; a transparent queue with named rules makes the counts auditable.

stages.description: Records with a thin or missing abstract are completed from OpenAlex, Crossref, Europe PMC and Semantic Scholar in that order; nothing already present is overwritten and every fetch is logged.
stages.title: Missing abstracts
stages.why: Ranking and screening read the abstract; a record without one is judged on its title alone, so it is easily ranked low or set aside.

stages.description: Every record is embedded and scored against the approved anchors (mean of its top cells). The ranking sorts, never filters. Seed-paper ranks, recall@K and tests without one part over anchor versions and embedding models show how well the anchors work; clusters in the top of the ranking describe the topics found.
stages.title: Ranking
stages.why: A ranking lets the human and LLM effort concentrate where relevant papers are dense, while a probability sample over the whole ranking keeps the recall estimate honest.

stages.description: A band-stratified probability sample (for the recall estimate) and a purposive development set (likely includes, near-misses per adjacent literature, cluster medoids, thin abstracts, tail) are drawn and labelled in the blinded queue by one or two reviewers.
stages.title: Samples and labelling
stages.why: Human labels on a known design are what make the LLM's recall measurable; the development set is where the prompt is tuned on the hardest cases.

stages.description: The codebook becomes a prompt and JSON schema; each record is screened in an isolated call that quotes the words behind every grade, and an "absent" grade whose quote is not in the record becomes unclear. Development-set evaluation reports misses per adjacent literature; the corpus protocol runs two passes, a blind third read on disagreement and a second screen of the maybes.
stages.title: Screening
stages.why: Verbatim quotes and a recall-first rule keep a small model from excluding on a hunch; repeated reads and a blind third read on disagreement catch some of its slips, and show where it answers inconsistently.

stages.description: Band-weighted recall of the LLM screen against the human labels, with an interval and the number of relevant papers, the PRISMA flow and a shareable report without abstracts.
stages.title: Recall and report
stages.why: The claim a review makes is "we found nearly all of it"; this stage puts a number and an interval on it.

stages.description: Stage-2 extension point.
stages.title: Full-text screening
stages.why: Abstract-level screening leaves the includes and maybes; reading their full texts is the next decision layer.

stages.description: Stage-2 extension point.
stages.title: Data extraction
stages.why: Once the set is final, the same codebook elements can be extracted per paper for the synthesis.

data.prompt:
You are screening one bibliographic record, by title and abstract only, for a systematic review. Decide whether the record could belong in the review.

# How to work

- Judge only from the title and abstract supplied. Do not use anything you may know about the paper, its authors or its journal. Never invent detail that is not in the text.
- Check the four elements one by one, answer the two checks, compare the study with the paper we are looking for, then decide.
- For every element, quote the words of the text that support your grade, verbatim. A quote is a copy of words from the title or abstract, never a sentence of your own: do not write "The abstract does not mention ..." in a quote field. A grade of "absent" is allowed only with a copied quote of the words that show the element is missing. If you cannot copy such words, leave the quote "" and grade "unclear".

# The paper we are looking for

Empirical studies of employees who voluntarily raise suggestions, concerns or problems with someone who could act on them (a supervisor, senior management, an internal or external authority), or who withhold such input, where the study measures what predicts that behaviour or what follows from it.

# The question

What leads employees to speak up, stay silent or report problems upward or outward at work, and what follows when they do?

# The four elements

A record is eligible when all four elements are plausibly present.

1. Voice, silence or reporting behaviour. The study measures employees speaking up, withholding input, or reporting problems. Counts: voice behaviour; speaking up; issue selling; upward communication; dissent; employee silence; whistleblowing. Does not count: a climate or culture measure alone; a composite citizenship scale in which voice is not analysed separately.2. Discretionary and directed upward or outward. The behaviour is the employee's own choice and is directed at someone who could act on it. Counts: informal suggestions to a supervisor; reports to a regulator or hotline. Does not count: formal participation schemes such as works councils; grievance procedures as the only channel; sharing information with peers only.3. Antecedents or consequences are studied. The study relates the behaviour to predictors, reactions or outcomes. Counts: predictors of voice or silence; receiver reactions; career, well-being or performance outcomes. Does not count: scale development with no substantive relation tested.4. Employees in work organisations. The actors are employees, members or contractors of an organisation. Counts: employees; nurses; crew members; students in a work placement. Does not count: customers or consumers; citizens addressing government; patients.Not a criterion: setting or industry; occupation; country; research method.

# Two checks, decided by the review author, that you must answer before deciding

1. voice_subscale_only. Is voice only one sub-dimension of a broader scale that is not analysed separately? If yes: maybe
2. formal_scheme_only. Does the study examine only a formal participation scheme or procedure? If yes: maybe

# Adjacent literatures that look like includes but are not

- participation schemes and industrial democracy (works councils, codetermination) (strains e2): exclude, reason b- grievance procedures as a formal channel (strains e2): maybe, reason b. include when the decision to file is studied as the employee's choice- organisational citizenship behaviour composites (strains e1): maybe, reason a. include when voice is analysed as a separate dimension- psychological safety as a climate construct (strains e1): maybe, reason a. include when voice or silence is also measured- customer and consumer complaining (strains e4): exclude, reason d- citizen participation and political voice (strains e4): exclude, reason d- peer information sharing and team communication (strains e2): exclude, reason b
# Edge cases, decided by the review author

- reviews and conceptual papers on the topic: maybe (edge_case "non_empirical")
- qualitative studies with no measured antecedent or outcome: maybe (edge_case "qualitative_only")

# The cells

If the record is an include, name the cell that fits its main question.

- voice_antecedent: what leads employees to speak up with suggestions or concerns
- voice_consequence: how receivers react to voice and what follows for the speaker
- silence_antecedent: why employees withhold concerns or opinions
- silence_consequence: what follows when employees stay silent
- whistleblowing_antecedent: what leads employees to report irregularities to an authority
- whistleblowing_consequence: what happens to employees after they report irregularities

# Decision

- include: all four elements are plausibly present from the title and abstract.
- exclude: only when the study is unrelated to the topic, or when you have graded an element absent with a quote of the words that show it. Give one reason: a, no voice, silence or reporting behaviour measured; b, not discretionary or not directed at someone who could act; c, no antecedent or consequence studied; d, actors are not employees; e, not empirical; f, too little information.- maybe: in every other case: you cannot tell from the text, a check says so, an edge case applies, the paper is non-empirical but on topic, or there is no usable abstract. Say what is missing.

# Output

Return only one JSON object with exactly these fields, in this order:

- summary: one sentence in your own words saying what the study did and what it compared. Not the title.
- e1: "present", "unclear" or "absent" for voice, silence or reporting behaviour.
- e1_quote: the words of the text your grade rests on, copied verbatim, or "" if none.
- e2: "present", "unclear" or "absent" for discretionary and directed upward or outward.
- e2_quote: the words of the text your grade rests on, copied verbatim, or "" if none.
- e3: "present", "unclear" or "absent" for antecedents or consequences are studied.
- e3_quote: the words of the text your grade rests on, copied verbatim, or "" if none.
- e4: "present", "unclear" or "absent" for employees in work organisations.
- e4_quote: the words of the text your grade rests on, copied verbatim, or "" if none.
- voice_subscale_only: true or false.
- formal_scheme_only: true or false.
- target_fit: "core" if this is the kind of study described above; "adjacent" if it is about the topic but an element is missing or unclear; "unrelated" if it is about neither.
- edge_case: "non_empirical", "qualitative_only" or "none".
- decision: "include", "maybe" or "exclude".
- exclusion_reason: "a", "b", "c", "d", "e", "f", or "none".
- missing_for_maybe: for a maybe, what the text does not say; otherwise "".
- cell: for an include, one of "voice_antecedent", "voice_consequence", "silence_antecedent", "silence_consequence", "whistleblowing_antecedent", "whistleblowing_consequence"; otherwise "not_applicable".
- target: for an include, one of "supervisor", "senior_management", "external_body", "peers"; otherwise "not_applicable".

stages.description: Write down the research question(s), the inclusion and exclusion notes, the seed papers (a development and a validation set), and the databases you will search. Everything later is checked against these inputs.
stages.title: Review plan
stages.why: A review of a broad construct drifts unless the question and the known-relevant papers are fixed first; the validation seed papers are held back so the search can be tested once, honestly.

stages.description: The LLM proposes, from your question and the development seed papers' abstracts, the construct cells, the screening codebook, synonym blocks for the query, one anchor sentence per cell, and near-miss (adjacent literature) descriptions. You edit and approve each; every version is kept.
stages.title: Concepts and synonyms
stages.why: Broad constructs are reviewed well only when their vocabulary and boundaries are written down before searching; grounding the proposals in your own seed papers keeps them specific to your literature.

stages.description: The approved synonym blocks are rendered into one Boolean string per chosen database, in that database's own syntax. You run the searches yourself and bring back the exports. Coverage of the development seed papers is checked while you edit; the validation set is reported only once the query is frozen or the uploads are marked final.
stages.title: Search strings
stages.why: Databases differ in syntax and limits; one shared query representation keeps the strings consistent and reproducible, and the freeze rule prevents tuning the query to the test papers.

stages.description: Database exports (RIS, CSV/TSV, XLS/XLSX or BibTeX, one folder per database) are recognised by their header, standardised and stored with their source file; a file is imported once, by content hash, and gets a sanity verdict (ok, capped, off-topic, empty, duplicate). Coverage then shows which seed papers each database returned (by DOI, exact title, then fuzzy title) and, after dedup, which the corpus holds.
stages.title: Search results
stages.why: An export that is not the result of your query (wrong search, truncated download) silently ruins recall; a seed paper missing from the database that should have found it is the cheapest warning you will get.

stages.description: Records are merged by DOI, then exact title, then fuzzy title with corroboration (year, first author, journal). Uncertain pairs go to a manual queue; your decisions are stored and re-applied. PRISMA counts and audit files are written.
stages.title: Deduplication
stages.why: Rules alone over-merge or under-merge; a transparent queue with named rules makes the counts auditable.

stages.description: Records with a thin or missing abstract are completed from OpenAlex, Crossref, Europe PMC and Semantic Scholar in that order; nothing already present is overwritten and every fetch is logged.
stages.title: Missing abstracts
stages.why: Ranking and screening read the abstract; a record without one is judged on its title alone, so it is easily ranked low or set aside.

stages.description: Every record is embedded and scored against the approved anchors (mean of its top cells). The ranking sorts, never filters. Seed-paper ranks, recall@K and tests without one part over anchor versions and embedding models show how well the anchors work; clusters in the top of the ranking describe the topics found.
stages.title: Ranking
stages.why: A ranking lets the human and LLM effort concentrate where relevant papers are dense, while a probability sample over the whole ranking keeps the recall estimate honest.

stages.description: A band-stratified probability sample (for the recall estimate) and a purposive development set (likely includes, near-misses per adjacent literature, cluster medoids, thin abstracts, tail) are drawn and labelled in the blinded queue by one or two reviewers.
stages.title: Samples and labelling
stages.why: Human labels on a known design are what make the LLM's recall measurable; the development set is where the prompt is tuned on the hardest cases.

stages.description: The codebook becomes a prompt and JSON schema; each record is screened in an isolated call that quotes the words behind every grade, and an "absent" grade whose quote is not in the record becomes unclear. Development-set evaluation reports misses per adjacent literature; the corpus protocol runs two passes, a blind third read on disagreement and a second screen of the maybes.
stages.title: Screening
stages.why: Verbatim quotes and a recall-first rule keep a small model from excluding on a hunch; repeated reads and a blind third read on disagreement catch some of its slips, and show where it answers inconsistently.

stages.description: Band-weighted recall of the LLM screen against the human labels, with an interval and the number of relevant papers, the PRISMA flow and a shareable report without abstracts.
stages.title: Recall and report
stages.why: The claim a review makes is "we found nearly all of it"; this stage puts a number and an interval on it.

stages.description: Stage-2 extension point.
stages.title: Full-text screening
stages.why: Abstract-level screening leaves the includes and maybes; reading their full texts is the next decision layer.

stages.description: Stage-2 extension point.
stages.title: Data extraction
stages.why: Once the set is final, the same codebook elements can be extracted per paper for the synthesis.

stages.description: Stage-2 extension point.
stages.title: Synthesis
stages.why: The extracted elements are what a synthesis of a wide literature is built from.
